sections.COMMENTS:
The westernmost Apennineâ€“Maghrebide thrust system is an EW contraction belt that runs across Sicily Island from Calabria to the Sicily Channel. This belt is made of folds and thrusts generated by the continental collision between the Africa and Eurasia Plates. The thrust fault planes dip both to the north and to the south. This belt is thought to accommodate 2-5 mm/y of the total Africa-Europe convergence (Dâ€™Agostino and Selvaggi, 2004; Serpelloni et al., 2007). In the on-land sector the recent activity of the thrust front is testified by the deformation of the Plio-Quaternary foredeep deposits and south of the Mt. Etna volcano, of late Pleistocene-Holocene marine and fluvial deposits. This contractional belt is connected with the Tell-Atlas thrust system in Tunisia across the Sicily Channel, where submerged contractional features coexist with the extensional horst and graben pattern of the Pelagian Foreland (Finetti and Del Ben, 2005; Corti et al., 2006).
Historical and instrumental catalogs show some 4.5 < Mw<5 events in western Sicily (SHEEC, Stucchi et al., 2012; EMEC, GrÃ¼nthal and WahlstrÃ¶m, 2012). The largest of them was that of 15 January 1968 (Mw 6.3). In the past 30 years several events with M>5 originated in the area off the northern coast of Sicily, including the Mw 5.9 Palermo earthquake of 2002. These last are mostly shallow compressional earthquakes with NNW-SSE P-axes (Goes et al., 2004; Pondrelli et al., 2004; Vannucci et al., 2004). This contraction trend is consistent with the plate motion vectors derived from GPS data.
This Composite Source belongs to the westernmost offshore portion of the Apennineâ€“Maghrebide thrust system. We constrained the strike of the source taking into account the geometry of the known fault traces and the orientation of geologic and geomorphic features (Finetti and Del Ben, 2005; Corti et al., 2006). We inferred average dip and rake of the source, along with slip rates, on the basis of regional tectonic and geodynamic considerations.
